name: Stone Soup
summary: UK Dstl's open Python framework for building and benchmarking multi-target trackers: Kalman/particle filters, data association, track initiation and metrics in composable components.
why_it_matters: A government-backed, permissively developed tracking toolkit - the closest thing to a reference library for situational-awareness fusion that defense judges will recognize.
hackathon_notes: pip install stonesoup; tutorials run in Jupyter. Good for fusing ADS-B, Remote ID or DF bearings into tracks on a common picture within a day. Keep it to air-picture awareness, not fire control.

name: Open Drone ID Core C
summary: Reference C library for encoding and decoding ASTM F3411 / ASD-STAN Remote ID messages (location, operator, system, auth) for Bluetooth and Wi-Fi broadcast.
why_it_matters: Remote ID is the cooperative layer of airspace awareness and counter-UAS; this library is the canonical message implementation.
hackathon_notes: Builds with CMake in minutes; pair with an ESP32 or phone receiver to decode drone broadcasts and push them to a map or TAK.

name: Open Drone ID Android Receiver
summary: Example Android app that listens for Remote ID broadcasts over Bluetooth 4/5 and Wi-Fi Beacon/NaN and shows drones and operators on a map.
why_it_matters: Fastest way to get a working cooperative drone-detection sensor in a hackathon using only phones.
hackathon_notes: Sideload on a recent Android phone; Wi-Fi NaN support depends on handset. Extend to forward detections as CoT to a TAK server.

name: ATAK-CIV (DoD release, archived)
summary: The DoD's public source release of the civilian Android Team Awareness Kit: map engine, Cursor-on-Target messaging and plugin SDK.
why_it_matters: TAK is the de facto common operating picture across US/NATO units, so a plugin or CoT feed is an instantly legible demo for defense judges.
hackathon_notes: Archived; use the TAK Product Center repo for current code. Building ATAK from source is heavy - develop a plugin against a prebuilt SDK instead.

name: ATAK-CIV (TAK Product Center)
summary: Current public home of the ATAK-CIV source and plugin examples maintained by the TAK Product Center.
why_it_matters: The place to start an ATAK plugin that visualizes PNT health, jamming reports or drone detections.
hackathon_notes: Plugin builds need the matching SDK version; budget half a day for toolchain. Many teams instead feed CoT from Python and just use stock ATAK/iTAK.

name: FreeTAKServer
summary: Open-source Python server that relays Cursor-on-Target traffic between TAK clients, with REST API and data packages.
why_it_matters: Lets a team stand up a shared situational-awareness network without access to the official TAK Server.
hackathon_notes: pip install or the ZeroTouch installer; activity slowed since 2024, so check OpenTAKServer as a more active option.

name: OpenTAKServer
summary: Actively maintained open TAK server for ATAK, iTAK and WinTAK with web UI, video streaming and Meshtastic integration.
why_it_matters: Quick, modern backend for a common operating picture demo linking several sensors and phones.
hackathon_notes: Installer scripts for Linux/RPi; get clients connected in an hour, then focus on your sensor feed.

name: PyTAK
summary: Python asyncio library for producing and consuming Cursor-on-Target messages and talking to TAK servers over TCP, UDP or TLS.
why_it_matters: The glue that turns any sensor script (GNSS monitor, Remote ID sniffer, DF array) into a TAK layer in a few lines.
hackathon_notes: pip install pytak; write a CoT generator for your detections. Lowest-friction way into the TAK ecosystem.

name: ADSBCOT
summary: Gateway that converts ADS-B traffic from dump1090/readsb or aggregator APIs into Cursor-on-Target so aircraft show in TAK.
why_it_matters: ADS-B also carries NIC/NACp integrity fields - the same signal GPSJam uses - so this is a ready bridge for a live GNSS-interference overlay.
hackathon_notes: Run alongside readsb on an RTL-SDR; add a filter that flags low NIC aircraft as an interference indicator.

name: readsb
summary: High-performance ADS-B/Mode S decoder for RTL-SDR and other receivers, used by most community feeder networks.
why_it_matters: Gives a team its own receiver for aircraft positions and navigation-integrity reports, the raw material for crowd-sourced jamming maps.
hackathon_notes: Install on a Pi with a cheap RTL-SDR and 1090 MHz antenna; JSON output is easy to parse for NIC/NACp statistics.

name: tar1090
summary: Web map interface for readsb/dump1090 with history, trails and per-aircraft details.
why_it_matters: Ready-made visualization layer for an ADS-B based interference or airspace-awareness demo.
hackathon_notes: One-line install on top of readsb. Fork the JS to color aircraft by NIC to show degraded GNSS.

name: dump1090-fa
summary: FlightAware's maintained Mode S/ADS-B decoder for RTL-SDR dongles.
why_it_matters: Widely packaged alternative to readsb for the same ADS-B situational-awareness use.
hackathon_notes: apt-installable on Raspberry Pi OS; pick either this or readsb, not both.

name: OpenWebRX
summary: Multi-user web SDR receiver with waterfall display and many built-in digital decoders.
why_it_matters: Shared, browser-based spectrum view is a simple way to demonstrate RF situational awareness, e.g. watching the GNSS L1 band for interference with a suitable front end.
hackathon_notes: Docker image available. Upstream activity slowed after 2024; the luarvique fork is more active.

name: OpenWebRX+
summary: Actively developed fork of OpenWebRX adding decoders, bookmarks and packaging improvements.
why_it_matters: Same browser spectrum-monitoring capability with current maintenance.
hackathon_notes: Use the provided packages/Docker; works with RTL-SDR, Airspy, SDRplay, HackRF.

name: Gqrx
summary: Desktop SDR receiver built on GNU Radio and Qt with FFT/waterfall and demodulators.
why_it_matters: Quick local spectrum inspection when characterizing a jammer test signal in a shielded lab or checking band occupancy.
hackathon_notes: Available via brew/apt. Only transmit-free monitoring; never radiate in GNSS bands outside licensed test ranges.

name: KrakenSDR DoA DSP
summary: Direction-of-arrival processing and web UI for the five-channel coherent KrakenSDR, producing bearings to RF emitters.
why_it_matters: Passive DF of interference sources (or drone control links) is a core defensive-EW capability and maps well to a hackathon demo.
hackathon_notes: Needs KrakenSDR hardware (or recorded IQ). Prebuilt Raspberry Pi images exist (check the KrakenRF docs). Multiple stations plus Stone Soup gives triangulated emitter tracks.

name: Heimdall DAQ firmware
summary: Coherent multichannel SDR acquisition chain (sync, calibration, decimation) underneath KrakenSDR DoA and passive radar apps.
why_it_matters: Useful if you need raw coherent IQ for your own DF or interference-localization algorithm.
hackathon_notes: Installed as part of the KrakenSDR image; modify only if building custom DSP.

name: DroneSecurity (DJI DroneID receiver)
summary: Code from the NDSS 2023 study that reverse-engineered DJI's proprietary DroneID broadcast and decodes it with an SDR.
why_it_matters: Shows how passive decoding of drone telemetry supports detection and localization of DJI aircraft, a common C-UAS need.
hackathon_notes: Requires a wideband SDR (e.g. USRP/BladeRF) and recorded or live captures; sample captures ease offline work.

name: DragonSync
summary: Gateway that takes drone Remote ID / DroneID detections from WarDragon-style sensors and publishes them as CoT to TAK and other outputs.
why_it_matters: Working example of a passive drone-detection to common-operating-picture pipeline.
hackathon_notes: Read it as a reference architecture even without the WarDragon kit; reuse its CoT mapping for your own detector.

name: drone-mesh-mapper
summary: ESP32 firmware and a Python/Flask mapper that capture Remote ID broadcasts over both BLE and Wi-Fi, relay detections over a Meshtastic LoRa mesh and plot drones and pilots on a live, offline-capable web map.
why_it_matters: Cheap, distributed, off-grid drone-awareness network - very hackathon friendly hardware.
hackathon_notes: ESP32 boards plus Meshtastic nodes cost little; flash and map in an afternoon.

name: MagNav.jl
summary: Julia package from the MIT/USAF AI Accelerator for airborne magnetic anomaly navigation: Tolles-Lawson and neural-net aircraft compensation, map handling and EKF/MPF navigation, with the challenge flight data.
why_it_matters: Official code behind the AFRL/MIT MagNav challenge; magnetic navigation is a leading GNSS-independent, unjammable PNT approach in DIU and AFRL programs.
hackathon_notes: Julia install plus large data download; first run compiles slowly. Start from the example notebooks and the provided flight lines.

name: MagNav challenge submission (lw-kong)
summary: A public submission repository for the JuliaCon 2020 MagNav signal-enhancement challenge, implementing a learned aircraft-field compensation.
why_it_matters: One of the few open challenge entries - shows what a competing compensation pipeline looks like end to end.
hackathon_notes: Inactive since 2022; useful as a template for a challenge-style submission on the MagNav data.

name: MagNav deep-learning compensation (naatyu)
summary: Notebooks applying deep learning to aircraft magnetic disturbance compensation on the MagNav challenge data.
why_it_matters: Python-first alternative for teams that do not want Julia.
hackathon_notes: Unmaintained since 2023; dependencies may need pinning.

name: MagNavPy
summary: Community Python port of MIT's MagNav.jl: loads flight, INS and magnetometer data and magnetic anomaly maps (with upward continuation), runs Tolles-Lawson and neural-network aircraft compensation, and provides an EKF / MagNav filter with CRLB analysis and plotting.
why_it_matters: Lowers the language barrier to the MagNav data and algorithms for Python-heavy teams.
hackathon_notes: Young community port; verify results against MagNav.jl outputs before trusting.

name: DARPA SubT Virtual Challenge
summary: Gazebo worlds, robot models, ROS interfaces and scoring tools from the virtual track of the DARPA Subterranean Challenge.
why_it_matters: Ready GNSS-denied underground environments with official scoring - a credible simulation testbed straight out of a DARPA challenge.
hackathon_notes: Dockerized, ROS1-era; heavy GPU/CPU needs. Use the hello-world repo as a starting point.

name: GBPlanner (CERBERUS)
summary: Graph-based exploration planner for subterranean environments, the planning core of Team CERBERUS, winner of the DARPA SubT final.
why_it_matters: Winning-team open code for autonomous exploration of GNSS-denied spaces with legged and aerial robots.
hackathon_notes: ROS1 catkin build with simulation demos; budget hours for dependencies. Pair with any lidar odometry.

name: MBPlanner
summary: Motion-primitive based exploration planner for fast aerial robots in confined spaces, used in CERBERUS flying platforms.
why_it_matters: Aerial complement to GBPlanner for drone exploration without GNSS.
hackathon_notes: ROS1, not updated since 2023.

name: LAMP (NeBula multi-robot SLAM)
summary: Team CoSTAR's large-scale multi-robot lidar SLAM back end with robust loop closure, from the NASA JPL-led SubT entry.
why_it_matters: Open component of the NeBula stack that won the SubT Urban circuit; shows multi-robot GNSS-denied mapping done at challenge scale.
hackathon_notes: ROS1 and dormant since 2023; run on the NeBula multi-robot dataset rather than live hardware.

name: NeBula multi-robot dataset
summary: Index for CoSTAR's multi-robot lidar/IMU/odometry datasets recorded in tunnels, mines and urban underground sites.
why_it_matters: Real GNSS-denied field data from SubT for testing SLAM or loop closure without building robots.
hackathon_notes: Bags are large; pick one sequence.

name: TARE Planner (CMU Explorer)
summary: Hierarchical exploration planner from CMU's Team Explorer, which earned the most-sectors-explored award at the SubT final.
why_it_matters: Well-documented, high-performing exploration planner that runs on top of a ready simulation stack.
hackathon_notes: Install the companion development environment first; ROS1 and ROS2 branches exist. Runs in sim on a laptop.

name: CMU Autonomous Exploration Development Environment
summary: Simulation worlds, local planner, terrain analysis and visualization used by CMU Explorer to develop ground-robot exploration.
why_it_matters: Fastest route to a GNSS-free autonomy demo: drop-in base for planners like TARE and FAR.
hackathon_notes: Works in ROS1 Noetic/ROS2 Humble; follow the website setup, environments download separately.

name: FAR Planner
summary: Visibility-graph route planner for known and unknown environments from the CMU SubT team.
why_it_matters: Long-range routing companion to exploration planners in GNSS-denied environments.
hackathon_notes: Runs in the same CMU development environment.

name: Time-optimal quadrotor planning
summary: Code for computing time-optimal quadrotor trajectories through waypoints, from the UZH group that placed second in AlphaPilot and built Swift.
why_it_matters: Insight into how top drone-racing teams plan; transferable to fast inspection or reconnaissance flight planning.
hackathon_notes: Python/CasADi, offline only. Inactive since 2021.

name: Flightmare
summary: Quadrotor simulator combining Unity rendering with a fast physics engine for RL and vision-based flight research.
why_it_matters: Simulation lineage behind UZH's drone-racing work; useful for training vision-based navigation without hardware.
hackathon_notes: Not updated since 2024; Unity build download required. Consider newer simulators if setup stalls.

name: SPEED+ baseline
summary: PyTorch baselines and domain-bridging methods for spacecraft pose estimation on the SPEED+ dataset used in ESA Kelvins SPEC2021.
why_it_matters: Open code tied to an ESA competition on vision-based relative navigation and sim-to-real gap.
hackathon_notes: Dataset download is large; start with a subset. Inactive since 2023.
